explanations.answer: Jesus had often met there with His disciples
explanations.explanation: John 18:2 says Judas knew the place because Jesus had often met there with His disciples. So it wasn't a secret spot. Judas had been there with them, and that's how he knew right where to bring everybody. I think that makes this one sting a little extra.

explanations.answer: The chief priests had shown him the way there
explanations.explanation: Nope, the text doesn't say the chief priests showed him anything. John 18:2 says Judas knew the place because Jesus had often met there with His disciples. Judas already had the directions in his head from being there himself. He didn't need a map from anybody.

explanations.answer: His family had once owned the land nearby
explanations.explanation: That one's not in the text, friend. John 18:2 gives the reason: Jesus had often met there with His disciples. Judas knew the garden because he had been in it with them, plain and simple. His family isn't even mentioned.

John 18:3 says the officers came from the chief priests and Pharisees. So these officers were sent by Jewish religious leaders, not by a king or a governor. The soldiers and officers walk into that garden together with Judas. That's quite a crowd for a quiet evening.

Not this time. John 18:3 says the officers came from the chief priests and Pharisees. Herod isn't in this passage at all. I'd have loved to see a whole royal court show up in a garden, though. Somebody would have to carry the throne.

The text doesn't send these officers from Caesar or a governor. John 18:3 says the officers came from the chief priests and Pharisees. Neither Caesar nor any governor is named in these verses. Just the priests and Pharisees, with Judas leading the way.

Yes, John 18:3 says they arrived carrying lanterns, torches, and weapons. That's not a casual walk in the garden. They came with light and they came ready. Think of someone showing up to borrow a cup of sugar with a whole toolbox.

John 18:3 says they arrived at the garden carrying lanterns, torches, and weapons. So the weapons are right there in the verse, next to the lights. This crowd didn't come empty-handed. They came loaded up, friend.

explanations.answer: Steps forward and asks who they are looking for
explanations.explanation: John 18:4 says Jesus, knowing all that was coming upon Him, stepped forward and asked, "Whom are you seeking?" He doesn't run and He doesn't hide. He walks right up to them. I'll be honest, I once hid from a smoke alarm. This is a different level.

explanations.answer: Slips back across the Kidron Valley in the dark
explanations.explanation: That's not what happens. John 18:4 says Jesus, knowing all that was coming upon Him, stepped forward and asked, "Whom are you seeking?" He moves toward them, not away. The valley stays right where it is behind Him.

explanations.answer: Hides deeper in the garden with His disciples
explanations.explanation: No hiding here, friend. John 18:4 says Jesus, knowing all that was coming upon Him, stepped forward and asked, "Whom are you seeking?" He steps out to meet them. Nobody has to go looking through the bushes.
Close, but no. In John 18:5 they say Jesus of Nazareth, and Jesus answers, "I am He." So He tells them they have the right man, not the wrong one. He doesn't dodge the question for a second.

That's right. They answer, "Jesus of Nazareth," and Jesus says, "I am He." (John 18:5) He owns it right there, no wrong man, no excuses. Most of us would have at least coughed and looked around first.
Yep. John 18:6 says when Jesus said, "I am He," they drew back and fell to the ground. The ones who came with weapons are the ones on the floor. I think I'd have dropped my whole tray of cookies.
John 18:6 says it plainly: when Jesus said, "I am He," they drew back and fell to the ground. So they don't stand firm or charge in. They go down. That's what the text says happened.

In John 18:8 Jesus says, "So if you are looking for Me, let these men go." He's the one they came for, and He speaks up for the men with Him. Right there in the middle of all those torches, He's thinking of them.
Jesus says the opposite. In John 18:8 He says, "So if you are looking for Me, let these men go." He points them to Himself and asks that His disciples be released. Nobody gets added to the list.
That's not what He says. John 18:8 has Jesus say, "So if you are looking for Me, let these men go." There's no questioning in His request. He just asks them to let His men go.

explanations.answer: I have not lost one of those You have given Me
explanations.explanation: The writer says it fulfills the word Jesus had spoken: "I have not lost one of those You have given Me." (John 18:9) The writer connects that word to Jesus speaking up for His disciples in the garden. Not one of them lost. That's a promise with some weight to it.

explanations.answer: Those You have given Me will stand with Me to the end
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but that's not the wording. John 18:9 says the word was, "I have not lost one of those You have given Me." The focus is on Jesus not losing any of them. It's not about them standing with Him.

explanations.answer: I will lead those You have given Me wherever You send
explanations.explanation: That sounds nice, but it's not in the verse. John 18:9 gives the word Jesus had spoken: "I have not lost one of those You have given Me." The writer says that's what was being fulfilled. Plain and exact, friend.

Not quite. In John 18:11 Jesus says, "Put your sword back in its sheath!" He tells Peter to put it away, not to stand his ground. Peter's swing ended up with a servant missing his right ear, so I think it was good advice.
Right. Jesus tells Peter, "Put your sword back in its sheath!" (John 18:11) That's the opposite of keeping it out. Peter had already swung it once, and Jesus tells him to stop.

Jesus says, "Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?" (John 18:11) The cup is something the Father has given Him. Jesus talks about it right after telling Peter to put the sword away. That's the whole moment right there.
The high priest does show up in this passage, since Malchus is his servant (John 18:10). But the cup isn't from him. Jesus says, "Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?" (John 18:11).
Good try, but the verse names someone else. Jesus says, "Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?" (John 18:11) The cup comes from the Father. The word "world" isn't in that line.
